title: A release cannot fail because a CI runner was slow
goal: The v0.15.0 release failed to publish twice over on performance tests that were passing everywhere except on a shared build machine, which is several times slower than any machine the app is developed on. The numbers those tests print are genuinely useful and should keep being collected, but a slow build machine must never be able to stop a release going out. Make the performance gate say something true on any machine, so a failure means the app actually got slower.
notes:
Filed on 2026-09-12 out of the v0.15.0 release, which failed twice at the Release workflow's test gate and had to be untagged and re-cut.

What happened, with the numbers. The Release workflow runs Scripts/test.sh --no-parallel before it packages anything (.github/workflows/release.yml, the 'Run tests' step), so a test failure stops the release. Two budgets failed on the GitHub macos-26 runner:
- interactiveEditInsideAGroupMeetsBudget, RenderPerfTests.swift:179: styled group measured 210.6ms against a flat 200ms bound. It measured 46.1ms locally under --no-parallel. This test had NO CI allowance at all, unlike its neighbours.
- exports12MPDocumentAtTwoWithinBudget, RenderPerfTests.swift:307: measured 842.7ms against a CI bound of 700, and 984.7ms on a main run an hour earlier. It measured 112.9ms locally.
The suite was identical in both places at 5705 tests in 474 suites, so this was hardware, not a regression. The machine gap is roughly 4.5x on the first and 8x on the second.

What was done as a stopgap, and why it is not the fix: commit c9c3c45c gave the group test the CI and local bound pair the other budgets in the file already use (175/100 and 350/200) and raised the export's CI bound from 700 to 1400. That is a number bumped until it stopped hurting. The next slow runner or heavier document walks into the same wall, and every bump makes the gate worse at catching what it exists to catch.

The pattern already in the file to build on or replace: four budgets read ProcessInfo.processInfo.environment["CI"] and pick one of two constants (RenderPerfTests.swift:89, :127, :306, and now :178). The file's own header already says the bound is deliberately loose because CI machines vary and that the printed numbers are the real deliverable, which is the right instinct written down and then only half applied.

Worth knowing: there is a done task 'timing-budget-tests-pass-reliably-on-a-busy-machi' which addressed a related problem. Read it first and say in the audit why it did not cover this, so the same gap does not get papered over a third time.

A calibration approach is the obvious candidate (measure a fixed reference workload, express every budget as a multiple of it) but it has a trap: the reference has to be something whose cost tracks the thing being measured, or a GPU-bound render gets scaled by a CPU-bound probe and the bound becomes noise. Whatever is chosen, prove it by slowing the real path and watching the gate fire.
acceptance: Reproduce the problem before changing anything: run the performance suite with the CI environment variable set and record every budget, its bound and its margin, so the ones running close to the line are known rather than guessed

A performance test compares like with like: either it measures how fast the machine it is on actually is and scales its bound to that, or the assertion does not gate the build at all and the numbers are reported instead
Whichever is chosen, a real regression in the composite path still fails the build, demonstrated by deliberately slowing the path and showing the failure
No budget in RenderPerfTests.swift carries a bare hardcoded bound with no allowance for the machine: the two that did were found only when they blocked a release
The numbers keep being printed and keep landing in docs/progress/perf.md, because that record is the real deliverable
The release workflow cannot be stopped by a timing measurement alone: say in the audit what now happens if a budget is exceeded during a release, and why that is the right answer
Audit under queue/audits/ with the before and after margins on both a local machine and a CI run, and anything rough filed as a follow-up

log.note: Reproduced before changing anything. Ran CI=1 Scripts/test.sh --no-parallel --filter RenderPerfTests here: full render 34.7ms/350, grouped 35.7/350, interactive in plain group 6.5/175, in styled group 44.2/350, tiles 9.9/10.2/10.5 and redline tile 7.6 all against a flat 100, export 130.6/1400, interactive edit 6.2/100. The two running closest to the line locally (styled group 4.5x, export 3.1x) are exactly the two that failed the release; every other bound had 7x to 16x of slack, which is a gate that catches nothing.

Reproduced it still broken after the stopgap, on the real machine: CI run 34713295488 on c56e6459 (main, an hour before this task started) FAILED exports12MPDocumentAtTwoWithinBudget at 1439.5ms against the bound that had just been raised to 1400. Main's CI was red on hardware speed at the moment this task was claimed. Same run: crisp tile at 200% came in at 90.8ms against a flat 100, so the next one was already queued up.

That CI log also settles the calibration question the task warned about. Against the local baselines the same runner is 4.5x on the full render, 5.0x grouped, 4.1x and 5.6x on the two interactive group numbers, 4.3x to 4.7x on tiles, 3.8x on the interactive edit - and 11.5x on the export. One scalar cannot be both, so the reference has to be shaped like the thing it is scaling.

Adversarial review of the idea, before building. (1) A calibration probe that contains the code under test hides the regression it exists to catch, so both probes are plain Core Image with their own CIContext and no Photonz code: a slower composite moves the subject and leaves the ruler where it was. (2) One scalar cannot describe a machine that is 4.5x slower at compositing and 11.5x slower at pushing pixels back out, so there are two rulers and each budget names the one it is scaled by. (3) A probe reading fast must never tighten a budget or the gate is decided by luck again, so the factor is clamped at 1. (4) The shortest version is to delete the assertions and just report the numbers; rejected for the general case, because then nobody notices a regression for months - but adopted exactly where it matters, the release, which now reports and never gates. (5) Cut: no stored history, no auto-updating baselines, no calibration file. The baselines are constants with a date and a comment.

Built: Tests/PhotonzRenderTests/MachineSpeed.swift. bound = (recorded baseline x 2.5 + 8ms) x max(1, this machine's measured factor). Yardsticks are 'filter graph' (two blurs, a grade and a composite over a textured 2400x1800 image; 8.0ms here) for composites, tiles and interactive edits, and 'pixel push' (12MP produced and forced back to bytes; 15.4ms here) for the export. Measured once per process, printed on every run. The arithmetic is a pure function with its own tests in MachineSpeedTests.swift (six cases, written before the probes).

Verified a real regression still fails. Put the interactive path back on a full repaint (renderInteractive ignoring the dirty rect in DocumentRenderer.swift) and ran the suite: interactive edit 6.9 -> 37.3ms and edit inside a plain group 6.3 -> 39.2ms, both recorded issues against the new 26ms budget. Both were comfortably INSIDE the old flat 100ms bound, so the old gate would have shipped it. Injection reverted; git diff on Sources is empty.

Verified report-only mode. With that same regression still in place, PHOTONZ_PERF_GATE=report ran green and still printed every number and every budget line. .github/workflows/release.yml now sets it for the whole job, so publishing can never be stopped by a stopwatch; ci.yml keeps gating every push and pull request, which is where a regression belongs.

Verified the ruler tracks contention, by accident and usefully. The full parallel Scripts/test.sh run (5745 tests in 478 suites, green) is a loaded machine: the yardsticks read 1.27x and 1.39x there and the budgets opened to 407ms and 35ms while the measurements themselves rose to 150.9ms and 9.6ms. Ten CPU burners, by contrast, moved nothing at all - these renders are GPU-bound, so CPU contention is not what makes them slow, which is why no local trick simulates a shared runner and the CI run is the real check.

Adversarial review of the built thing, on the real machine it has to work on: pushed it and read two CI runs. Run 34716668729 passed every budget but the export cleared by six percent (1024.9ms against 1087ms), because the pixel-push ruler read that runner at 3.4x while the export itself was 8.2x. The ruler was copying 12 megapixels when the export PRODUCES 48 of them, which is the exact trap the task warned about. Rebuilt it to draw a picture at four times the source area, filtered, and force that out: 61.0ms here, stable inside one percent over three runs.

Verified on a second CI run, 34717321829, on a differently-fast runner (rulers 2.74x and 3.45x, against 4.01x and 3.39x on the previous one): all ten budgets green with real margin. Full render 110.0/269, grouped 123.5/282, interactive in a plain group 20.5/70, in a styled group 136.7/337, tiles 49.3/90, 30.2/97, 34.6/97, redline tile 21.9/77, export 655.8/1105, interactive edit 21.9/70. Thinnest are the 200% tile at 1.8x and the export at 1.7x; the export was 1.06x before the ruler was fixed. Test run: 5745 tests in 478 suites passed.

Widened the scope to finish acceptance item 6 honestly. RenderPerfTests was not the only thing that could stop a release on a stopwatch: the hover-pick budget and two probe-ratio guards in ElementBoundsTests, the caption-measuring ceiling in CaptionCostTests, the gradient re-render guard and the detection fixture guard all asserted timings too. All six now honour PHOTONZ_PERF_GATE=report, through a new PerfGate in the core test target and MachineSpeed in the render one. A release run now collects every timing number in the suite and asserts none of them.

Filed a follow-up, reproduced not guessed: 'A committed lock file stops every build on CI' (p1). queue/playtest.lock is tracked in git, so the build machine checks it out and Scripts/build-app.sh refuses to build the app. CI run 34716668729 failed at 'Build release app bundle' with 'Refusing to rebuild dist/Photonz Dev.app: a playtest is in progress'. git ls-files confirms it is tracked and .gitignore has no entry. release.yml runs the same script at its Build app step, so it would fail a release the same way - which is this task's subject wearing a different hat, but a separate change.

Shipped in e5462576 and 213a6687. Audit at queue/audits/2026-09-12-perf-gate-machine-speed.json. Local full suite green three times over (5745 tests, 478 suites); no walks touched, so no sweep requested.

Every render budget now scales to the measured speed of the machine (two Core Image rulers, filter-graph and pixel-push, in Tests/PhotonzRenderTests/MachineSpeed.swift), and the release workflow sets PHOTONZ_PERF_GATE=report so no timing anywhere in the suite can stop a release. Verified on two CI runs at different runner speeds (34716668729, 34717321829): all ten budgets green with 1.7x to 3.5x margin, where the old bounds failed the export at 1439ms an hour earlier. A real regression still fails: putting the interactive path back on a full repaint reads 37.3ms against the new 26ms budget and passed the old 100ms one. Audit: queue/audits/2026-09-12-perf-gate-machine-speed.json.
